newsitem.title: USA: Anti-blood clot drug seen better than aspirin.
newsitem.headline: Anti-blood clot drug seen better than aspirin.

text.p: A clinical study showed that a drug being developed by Elf Sanofi SA and Bristol-Myers Squibb Co works somewhat better than aspirin at reducing risks of stroke, heart attacks or death due to cardiovascular problems, researchers said on Wednesday.
The drug, clopidogrel, did not provoke the kind of stomach bleeding seen with aspirin, researchers said.

The so-called Caprie study showed that patients receiving clopidogrel had an overall reduced risk for stroke, heart attack and death due to cardiovascular problems of 8.7 percent over those treated with aspirin, the researchers said.

The study compared clopidogrel, which has the brand name Plavix, versus aspirin in 19,185 patients in 16 countries who had previously suffered a stroke, heart attack or had diseased arteries in the legs. Researchers described the study as the largest yet on any medicine not yet on the market.
The patients received either clopidogrel, an anti-platlet blood-clot fighting agent, or aspirin, commonly prescribed by doctors for preventing blood clots.
The patients took the drugs daily for about two years.

Aspirin reduces the number of strokes, heart attacks or death due to cardiovascular problems by one-quarter, while the study showed that clopidogrel reduces the number of those events by about a third, researchers said.

John Dormandy, a study investigator and professor of vascular sciences at London's St. George's Hospital Medical School, said there are about 20 million people in the U.S. at risk for the three events. An 8.7 percent improvement over aspirin could reduce the number of strokes, heart attacks or deaths due to cardiovascular problems by about 100,000 a year, he said.
Clopidogrel is a derivative of another Sanofi drug, ticlopidine, or Ticlid. Ticlopidine works about 10 percent better than aspirin but causes side effects including rashes and diarrhea.

"We were hoping to see a benefit (with clopidogrel) of about 10 percent better than asprin, but we were hoping to find a much safer drug," said Michael Gent, chairman of the Caprie steering committee, and director of the department of clinical epidemiology and biostatistics at McMaster University in Hamilton, Canada.
The resulting risk reduction from clopidogrel was "very close to where we targeted," Gent told a news conference.
Gent said the price of clopdiogrel has not been set.
Sanofi discovered clopidogrel and is developing the drug with Bristol-Myers in the U.S. and Europe. Upon its regulatory approval, both will market and promote the drug.
A Sanofi spokesmen said a filing for marketing approval of clopidogrel with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration was targeted for the first quarter of 1997.
